case_info.scenario: A 72-year-old woman with metastatic, well-differentiated, small intestinal neuroendocrine tumor (NET) presented for routine follow-up in September 2020 with worsening fatigue and flushing. She was initially diagnosed with metastatic involvement of the liver, bone, and intra-abdominal lymph nodes in 2015 and received 3 treatments with peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) in 2017. After 2 years of disease stability she was retreated with PRRT in November 2019 because of radiographic progression of disease and worsening symptoms. A third dose of PRRT was given in March 2020; a fourth was deferred owing to persistent thrombocytopenia after treatment. Gallium 68 dotatate positron emission tomography–computed tomography in July 2020 revealed stable disease (Figure, A). Laboratory results from the clinic visit noted a hemoglobin level of 7.5 g/dL (red cell distribution width, 63.2 fL), platelet count of 54 ×103/μL, and absolute neutrophil count of 1310/μL. (To convert hemoglobin to grams per liter, multiply by 10; platelet and absolute neutrophil counts to ×109/L, by 0.001.) Results of a peripheral blood smear did not suggest the presence of circulating blasts or schistocytes. She was referred to the hematologic malignancies clinic for evaluation. An extensive laboratory workup assessing nutritional deficiencies, viral exposure, and autoimmune disease was unrevealing. Hematopathology slides of a subsequent bone marrow biopsy specimen revealed tumor cells staining strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin (Figure, B) and chromogranin (Figure, C).

Each hyperdense area, except the physiologic uptake in the pituitary gland and bladder (arrowheads), corresponds to a NET deposit. B and C, Photomicrographs from the bone marrow biopsy specimen show the presence of tumor cells (arrowheads) staining strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin (original magnification ×20).
case_info.explanation: C. Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow Hematopathologic analysis revealed a mildly hypocellular marrow (10%-20% cellularity) with erythroid predominant trilineage hematopoiesis. No overt morphologic dysplasia or blasts were recognized; however, multiple aggregates of tumor cells that stained strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin were noted, which confirmed metastatic involvement of the NET in the bone marrow. Reports of bone marrow metastases from well-differentiated NETs are rare; we found only 5 cases in the literature since 2009.1Patients with solid tumor metastases to bone marrow typically present with thrombocytopenia, anemia, and elevated red cell distribution width and carry a poor prognosis.2For this patient, extensive bone involvement from her NET may have predisposed her to develop bone marrow infiltration; this association, however, has not been described in patients with NET and diffuse bone metastases. Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) is a devastating but infrequent complication of PRRT. The incidence of t-MDS with PRRT is estimated to be 2% to 5%, with a median time to onset after the completion of treatment from 12 to 78 months.3Potential risk factors that predispose patients with NETs to t-MDS, such as use of alkylating agents, presence of bone metastases, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation, have been inconsistently implicated across studies.4Patients with certain somatic mutations or clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential may be more inclined to develop t-MDS after PRRT; however, this association remains understudied.5There does not appear to be a dose effect; patients receiving retreatment with PRRT do not appear to have increased incidence of t-MDS compared with PRRT-naive patients.6The prognosis of patients who develop t-MDS is dismal, with median overall survival times just beyond 1 year from the time of diagnosis.3 Hematologic toxic effects of PRRT are typically subacute and reversible. In the randomized NETTER-1 study,7which garnered PRRT its approval for patients with progressive gastroenteropancreatic NETs, the most frequent grade 3 and 4 hematologic adverse events (AEs) were lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia in 9%, 2%, and 1% of cases, respectively.7None of the hematologic AEs were permanent. In a large observational cohort study of more than 600 patients with gastroenteropancreatic and bronchial NETs who underwent PRRT, 10% of patients experienced grade 3 or 4 hematologic AEs.8The most common of these AEs were thrombocytopenia (5% of cases), leukopenia (5%), and anemia (4%). Within 3 months of follow-up, 77% of these AEs resolved. Some cohort studies, however, suggest that hematologic AEs experienced by patients during PRRT can take longer to resolve.9 Aplastic anemia, characterized by a loss of hematopoietic stem cells, typically occurs because of toxins, viral syndromes, immune destruction, or underlying genetic syndromes.10Marrow toxic agents include some antimicrobial therapies (eg, chloramphenicol), chemotherapy, or high doses of ionizing radiation. Although this patient received ionizing radiation via PRRT, her bone marrow had only mild hypocellularity and no dysplastic features. In the setting of progressive disease, absence of other cytoreductive options and high tumor programmed death-ligand 1 expression, the patient began immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with pembrolizumab. Her anemia and thrombocytopenia are being managed with regular transfusions while disease response reassessment is pending.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       is ruled out already qualifies.

       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.

     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

A 72-year-old woman with metastatic, well-differentiated, small intestinal neuroendocrine tumor (NET) presented for routine follow-up in September 2020 with worsening fatigue and flushing. She was initially diagnosed with metastatic involvement of the liver, bone, and intra-abdominal lymph nodes in 2015 and received 3 treatments with peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) in 2017. After 2 years of disease stability she was retreated with PRRT in November 2019 because of radiographic progression of disease and worsening symptoms. A third dose of PRRT was given in March 2020; a fourth was deferred owing to persistent thrombocytopenia after treatment. Gallium 68 dotatate positron emission tomography–computed tomography in July 2020 revealed stable disease (Figure, A). Laboratory results from the clinic visit noted a hemoglobin level of 7.5 g/dL (red cell distribution width, 63.2 fL), platelet count of 54 ×103/μL, and absolute neutrophil count of 1310/μL. (To convert hemoglobin to grams per liter, multiply by 10; platelet and absolute neutrophil counts to ×109/L, by 0.001.) Results of a peripheral blood smear did not suggest the presence of circulating blasts or schistocytes. She was referred to the hematologic malignancies clinic for evaluation. An extensive laboratory workup assessing nutritional deficiencies, viral exposure, and autoimmune disease was unrevealing. Hematopathology slides of a subsequent bone marrow biopsy specimen revealed tumor cells staining strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin (Figure, B) and chromogranin (Figure, C).

case_info.explanation: C. Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow Hematopathologic analysis revealed a mildly hypocellular marrow (10%-20% cellularity) with erythroid predominant trilineage hematopoiesis. No overt morphologic dysplasia or blasts were recognized; however, multiple aggregates of tumor cells that stained strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin were noted, which confirmed metastatic involvement of the NET in the bone marrow. Reports of bone marrow metastases from well-differentiated NETs are rare; we found only 5 cases in the literature since 2009.1Patients with solid tumor metastases to bone marrow typically present with thrombocytopenia, anemia, and elevated red cell distribution width and carry a poor prognosis.2For this patient, extensive bone involvement from her NET may have predisposed her to develop bone marrow infiltration; this association, however, has not been described in patients with NET and diffuse bone metastases. Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) is a devastating but infrequent complication of PRRT. The incidence of t-MDS with PRRT is estimated to be 2% to 5%, with a median time to onset after the completion of treatment from 12 to 78 months.3Potential risk factors that predispose patients with NETs to t-MDS, such as use of alkylating agents, presence of bone metastases, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation, have been inconsistently implicated across studies.4Patients with certain somatic mutations or clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential may be more inclined to develop t-MDS after PRRT; however, this association remains understudied.5There does not appear to be a dose effect; patients receiving retreatment with PRRT do not appear to have increased incidence of t-MDS compared with PRRT-naive patients.6The prognosis of patients who develop t-MDS is dismal, with median overall survival times just beyond 1 year from the time of diagnosis.3 Hematologic toxic effects of PRRT are typically subacute and reversible. In the randomized NETTER-1 study,7which garnered PRRT its approval for patients with progressive gastroenteropancreatic NETs, the most frequent grade 3 and 4 hematologic adverse events (AEs) were lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia in 9%, 2%, and 1% of cases, respectively.7None of the hematologic AEs were permanent. In a large observational cohort study of more than 600 patients with gastroenteropancreatic and bronchial NETs who underwent PRRT, 10% of patients experienced grade 3 or 4 hematologic AEs.8The most common of these AEs were thrombocytopenia (5% of cases), leukopenia (5%), and anemia (4%). Within 3 months of follow-up, 77% of these AEs resolved. Some cohort studies, however, suggest that hematologic AEs experienced by patients during PRRT can take longer to resolve.9 Aplastic anemia, characterized by a loss of hematopoietic stem cells, typically occurs because of toxins, viral syndromes, immune destruction, or underlying genetic syndromes.10Marrow toxic agents include some antimicrobial therapies (eg, chloramphenicol), chemotherapy, or high doses of ionizing radiation. Although this patient received ionizing radiation via PRRT, her bone marrow had only mild hypocellularity and no dysplastic features. In the setting of progressive disease, absence of other cytoreductive options and high tumor programmed death-ligand 1 expression, the patient began immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with pembrolizumab. Her anemia and thrombocytopenia are being managed with regular transfusions while disease response reassessment is pending.

case_info.explanation: C. Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow Hematopathologic analysis revealed a mildly hypocellular marrow (10%-20% cellularity) with erythroid predominant trilineage hematopoiesis. No overt morphologic dysplasia or blasts were recognized; however, multiple aggregates of tumor cells that stained strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin were noted, which confirmed metastatic involvement of the NET in the bone marrow. Reports of bone marrow metastases from well-differentiated NETs are rare; we found only 5 cases in the literature since 2009.1Patients with solid tumor metastases to bone marrow typically present with thrombocytopenia, anemia, and elevated red cell distribution width and carry a poor prognosis.2For this patient, extensive bone involvement from her NET may have predisposed her to develop bone marrow infiltration; this association, however, has not been described in patients with NET and diffuse bone metastases. Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) is a devastating but infrequent complication of PRRT. The incidence of t-MDS with PRRT is estimated to be 2% to 5%, with a median time to onset after the completion of treatment from 12 to 78 months.3Potential risk factors that predispose patients with NETs to t-MDS, such as use of alkylating agents, presence of bone metastases, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation, have been inconsistently implicated across studies.4Patients with certain somatic mutations or clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential may be more inclined to develop t-MDS after PRRT; however, this association remains understudied.5There does not appear to be a dose effect; patients receiving retreatment with PRRT do not appear to have increased incidence of t-MDS compared with PRRT-naive patients.6The prognosis of patients who develop t-MDS is dismal, with median overall survival times just beyond 1 year from the time of diagnosis.3 Hematologic toxic effects of PRRT are typically subacute and reversible. In the randomized NETTER-1 study,7which garnered PRRT its approval for patients with progressive gastroenteropancreatic NETs, the most frequent grade 3 and 4 hematologic adverse events (AEs) were lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia in 9%, 2%, and 1% of cases, respectively.7None of the hematologic AEs were permanent. In a large observational cohort study of more than 600 patients with gastroenteropancreatic and bronchial NETs who underwent PRRT, 10% of patients experienced grade 3 or 4 hematologic AEs.8The most common of these AEs were thrombocytopenia (5% of cases), leukopenia (5%), and anemia (4%). Within 3 months of follow-up, 77% of these AEs resolved. Some cohort studies, however, suggest that hematologic AEs experienced by patients during PRRT can take longer to resolve.9 Aplastic anemia, characterized by a loss of hematopoietic stem cells, typically occurs because of toxins, viral syndromes, immune destruction, or underlying genetic syndromes.10Marrow toxic agents include some antimicrobial therapies (eg, chloramphenicol), chemotherapy, or high doses of ionizing radiation. Although this patient received ionizing radiation via PRRT, her bone marrow had only mild hypocellularity and no dysplastic features. In the setting of progressive disease, absence of other cytoreductive options and high tumor programmed death-ligand 1 expression, the patient began immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with pembrolizumab. Her anemia and thrombocytopenia are being managed with regular transfusions while disease response reassessment is pending.

case_info.caption: A, A July 2020 gallium 68 dotatate positron emission tomography–computed tomography image shows extensive but stable disease from the patient’s metastatic neuroendocrine tumor (NET). Each hyperdense area, except the physiologic uptake in the pituitary gland and bladder (arrowheads), corresponds to a NET deposit. B and C, Photomicrographs from the bone marrow biopsy specimen show the presence of tumor cells (arrowheads) staining strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin (original magnification ×20).
case_info.explanation: C. Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow Hematopathologic analysis revealed a mildly hypocellular marrow (10%-20% cellularity) with erythroid predominant trilineage hematopoiesis. No overt morphologic dysplasia or blasts were recognized; however, multiple aggregates of tumor cells that stained strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin were noted, which confirmed metastatic involvement of the NET in the bone marrow. Reports of bone marrow metastases from well-differentiated NETs are rare; we found only 5 cases in the literature since 2009.1Patients with solid tumor metastases to bone marrow typically present with thrombocytopenia, anemia, and elevated red cell distribution width and carry a poor prognosis.2For this patient, extensive bone involvement from her NET may have predisposed her to develop bone marrow infiltration; this association, however, has not been described in patients with NET and diffuse bone metastases. Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) is a devastating but infrequent complication of PRRT. The incidence of t-MDS with PRRT is estimated to be 2% to 5%, with a median time to onset after the completion of treatment from 12 to 78 months.3Potential risk factors that predispose patients with NETs to t-MDS, such as use of alkylating agents, presence of bone metastases, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation, have been inconsistently implicated across studies.4Patients with certain somatic mutations or clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential may be more inclined to develop t-MDS after PRRT; however, this association remains understudied.5There does not appear to be a dose effect; patients receiving retreatment with PRRT do not appear to have increased incidence of t-MDS compared with PRRT-naive patients.6The prognosis of patients who develop t-MDS is dismal, with median overall survival times just beyond 1 year from the time of diagnosis.3 Hematologic toxic effects of PRRT are typically subacute and reversible. In the randomized NETTER-1 study,7which garnered PRRT its approval for patients with progressive gastroenteropancreatic NETs, the most frequent grade 3 and 4 hematologic adverse events (AEs) were lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia in 9%, 2%, and 1% of cases, respectively.7None of the hematologic AEs were permanent. In a large observational cohort study of more than 600 patients with gastroenteropancreatic and bronchial NETs who underwent PRRT, 10% of patients experienced grade 3 or 4 hematologic AEs.8The most common of these AEs were thrombocytopenia (5% of cases), leukopenia (5%), and anemia (4%). Within 3 months of follow-up, 77% of these AEs resolved. Some cohort studies, however, suggest that hematologic AEs experienced by patients during PRRT can take longer to resolve.9 Aplastic anemia, characterized by a loss of hematopoietic stem cells, typically occurs because of toxins, viral syndromes, immune destruction, or underlying genetic syndromes.10Marrow toxic agents include some antimicrobial therapies (eg, chloramphenicol), chemotherapy, or high doses of ionizing radiation. Although this patient received ionizing radiation via PRRT, her bone marrow had only mild hypocellularity and no dysplastic features. In the setting of progressive disease, absence of other cytoreductive options and high tumor programmed death-ligand 1 expression, the patient began immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with pembrolizumab. Her anemia and thrombocytopenia are being managed with regular transfusions while disease response reassessment is pending.

case_info.explanation: C. Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow Hematopathologic analysis revealed a mildly hypocellular marrow (10%-20% cellularity) with erythroid predominant trilineage hematopoiesis. No overt morphologic dysplasia or blasts were recognized; however, multiple aggregates of tumor cells that stained strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin were noted, which confirmed metastatic involvement of the NET in the bone marrow. Reports of bone marrow metastases from well-differentiated NETs are rare; we found only 5 cases in the literature since 2009.1Patients with solid tumor metastases to bone marrow typically present with thrombocytopenia, anemia, and elevated red cell distribution width and carry a poor prognosis.2For this patient, extensive bone involvement from her NET may have predisposed her to develop bone marrow infiltration; this association, however, has not been described in patients with NET and diffuse bone metastases. Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) is a devastating but infrequent complication of PRRT. The incidence of t-MDS with PRRT is estimated to be 2% to 5%, with a median time to onset after the completion of treatment from 12 to 78 months.3Potential risk factors that predispose patients with NETs to t-MDS, such as use of alkylating agents, presence of bone metastases, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation, have been inconsistently implicated across studies.4Patients with certain somatic mutations or clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential may be more inclined to develop t-MDS after PRRT; however, this association remains understudied.5There does not appear to be a dose effect; patients receiving retreatment with PRRT do not appear to have increased incidence of t-MDS compared with PRRT-naive patients.6The prognosis of patients who develop t-MDS is dismal, with median overall survival times just beyond 1 year from the time of diagnosis.3 Hematologic toxic effects of PRRT are typically subacute and reversible. In the randomized NETTER-1 study,7which garnered PRRT its approval for patients with progressive gastroenteropancreatic NETs, the most frequent grade 3 and 4 hematologic adverse events (AEs) were lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia in 9%, 2%, and 1% of cases, respectively.7None of the hematologic AEs were permanent. In a large observational cohort study of more than 600 patients with gastroenteropancreatic and bronchial NETs who underwent PRRT, 10% of patients experienced grade 3 or 4 hematologic AEs.8The most common of these AEs were thrombocytopenia (5% of cases), leukopenia (5%), and anemia (4%). Within 3 months of follow-up, 77% of these AEs resolved. Some cohort studies, however, suggest that hematologic AEs experienced by patients during PRRT can take longer to resolve.9 Aplastic anemia, characterized by a loss of hematopoietic stem cells, typically occurs because of toxins, viral syndromes, immune destruction, or underlying genetic syndromes.10Marrow toxic agents include some antimicrobial therapies (eg, chloramphenicol), chemotherapy, or high doses of ionizing radiation. Although this patient received ionizing radiation via PRRT, her bone marrow had only mild hypocellularity and no dysplastic features. In the setting of progressive disease, absence of other cytoreductive options and high tumor programmed death-ligand 1 expression, the patient began immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with pembrolizumab. Her anemia and thrombocytopenia are being managed with regular transfusions while disease response reassessment is pending.

Hematopathology slides of a subsequent bone marrow biopsy specimen revealed tumor cells staining strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin (Figure, B) and chromogranin (Figure, C).

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: C. Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow Hematopathologic analysis revealed a mildly hypocellular marrow (10%-20% cellularity) with erythroid predominant trilineage hematopoiesis. No overt morphologic dysplasia or blasts were recognized; however, multiple aggregates of tumor cells that stained strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin were noted, which confirmed metastatic involvement of the NET in the bone marrow. Reports of bone marrow metastases from well-differentiated NETs are rare; we found only 5 cases in the literature since 2009.1Patients with solid tumor metastases to bone marrow typically present with thrombocytopenia, anemia, and elevated red cell distribution width and carry a poor prognosis.2For this patient, extensive bone involvement from her NET may have predisposed her to develop bone marrow infiltration; this association, however, has not been described in patients with NET and diffuse bone metastases. Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) is a devastating but infrequent complication of PRRT. The incidence of t-MDS with PRRT is estimated to be 2% to 5%, with a median time to onset after the completion of treatment from 12 to 78 months.3Potential risk factors that predispose patients with NETs to t-MDS, such as use of alkylating agents, presence of bone metastases, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation, have been inconsistently implicated across studies.4Patients with certain somatic mutations or clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential may be more inclined to develop t-MDS after PRRT; however, this association remains understudied.5There does not appear to be a dose effect; patients receiving retreatment with PRRT do not appear to have increased incidence of t-MDS compared with PRRT-naive patients.6The prognosis of patients who develop t-MDS is dismal, with median overall survival times just beyond 1 year from the time of diagnosis.3 Hematologic toxic effects of PRRT are typically subacute and reversible. In the randomized NETTER-1 study,7which garnered PRRT its approval for patients with progressive gastroenteropancreatic NETs, the most frequent grade 3 and 4 hematologic adverse events (AEs) were lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia in 9%, 2%, and 1% of cases, respectively.7None of the hematologic AEs were permanent. In a large observational cohort study of more than 600 patients with gastroenteropancreatic and bronchial NETs who underwent PRRT, 10% of patients experienced grade 3 or 4 hematologic AEs.8The most common of these AEs were thrombocytopenia (5% of cases), leukopenia (5%), and anemia (4%). Within 3 months of follow-up, 77% of these AEs resolved. Some cohort studies, however, suggest that hematologic AEs experienced by patients during PRRT can take longer to resolve.9 Aplastic anemia, characterized by a loss of hematopoietic stem cells, typically occurs because of toxins, viral syndromes, immune destruction, or underlying genetic syndromes.10Marrow toxic agents include some antimicrobial therapies (eg, chloramphenicol), chemotherapy, or high doses of ionizing radiation. Although this patient received ionizing radiation via PRRT, her bone marrow had only mild hypocellularity and no dysplastic features. In the setting of progressive disease, absence of other cytoreductive options and high tumor programmed death-ligand 1 expression, the patient began immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with pembrolizumab. Her anemia and thrombocytopenia are being managed with regular transfusions while disease response reassessment is pending.

case_info.explanation: C. Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow Hematopathologic analysis revealed a mildly hypocellular marrow (10%-20% cellularity) with erythroid predominant trilineage hematopoiesis. No overt morphologic dysplasia or blasts were recognized; however, multiple aggregates of tumor cells that stained strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin were noted, which confirmed metastatic involvement of the NET in the bone marrow. Reports of bone marrow metastases from well-differentiated NETs are rare; we found only 5 cases in the literature since 2009.1Patients with solid tumor metastases to bone marrow typically present with thrombocytopenia, anemia, and elevated red cell distribution width and carry a poor prognosis.2For this patient, extensive bone involvement from her NET may have predisposed her to develop bone marrow infiltration; this association, however, has not been described in patients with NET and diffuse bone metastases. Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) is a devastating but infrequent complication of PRRT. The incidence of t-MDS with PRRT is estimated to be 2% to 5%, with a median time to onset after the completion of treatment from 12 to 78 months.3Potential risk factors that predispose patients with NETs to t-MDS, such as use of alkylating agents, presence of bone metastases, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation, have been inconsistently implicated across studies.4Patients with certain somatic mutations or clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential may be more inclined to develop t-MDS after PRRT; however, this association remains understudied.5There does not appear to be a dose effect; patients receiving retreatment with PRRT do not appear to have increased incidence of t-MDS compared with PRRT-naive patients.6The prognosis of patients who develop t-MDS is dismal, with median overall survival times just beyond 1 year from the time of diagnosis.3 Hematologic toxic effects of PRRT are typically subacute and reversible. In the randomized NETTER-1 study,7which garnered PRRT its approval for patients with progressive gastroenteropancreatic NETs, the most frequent grade 3 and 4 hematologic adverse events (AEs) were lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia in 9%, 2%, and 1% of cases, respectively.7None of the hematologic AEs were permanent. In a large observational cohort study of more than 600 patients with gastroenteropancreatic and bronchial NETs who underwent PRRT, 10% of patients experienced grade 3 or 4 hematologic AEs.8The most common of these AEs were thrombocytopenia (5% of cases), leukopenia (5%), and anemia (4%). Within 3 months of follow-up, 77% of these AEs resolved. Some cohort studies, however, suggest that hematologic AEs experienced by patients during PRRT can take longer to resolve.9 Aplastic anemia, characterized by a loss of hematopoietic stem cells, typically occurs because of toxins, viral syndromes, immune destruction, or underlying genetic syndromes.10Marrow toxic agents include some antimicrobial therapies (eg, chloramphenicol), chemotherapy, or high doses of ionizing radiation. Although this patient received ionizing radiation via PRRT, her bone marrow had only mild hypocellularity and no dysplastic features. In the setting of progressive disease, absence of other cytoreductive options and high tumor programmed death-ligand 1 expression, the patient began immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with pembrolizumab. Her anemia and thrombocytopenia are being managed with regular transfusions while disease response reassessment is pending.

case_info.caption: A, A July 2020 gallium 68 dotatate positron emission tomography–computed tomography image shows extensive but stable disease from the patient’s metastatic neuroendocrine tumor (NET). Each hyperdense area, except the physiologic uptake in the pituitary gland and bladder (arrowheads), corresponds to a NET deposit. case_info.explanation: C. Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow Hematopathologic analysis revealed a mildly hypocellular marrow (10%-20% cellularity) with erythroid predominant trilineage hematopoiesis. No overt morphologic dysplasia or blasts were recognized; however, multiple aggregates of tumor cells that stained strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin were noted, which confirmed metastatic involvement of the NET in the bone marrow. Reports of bone marrow metastases from well-differentiated NETs are rare; we found only 5 cases in the literature since 2009.1Patients with solid tumor metastases to bone marrow typically present with thrombocytopenia, anemia, and elevated red cell distribution width and carry a poor prognosis.2For this patient, extensive bone involvement from her NET may have predisposed her to develop bone marrow infiltration; this association, however, has not been described in patients with NET and diffuse bone metastases. Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) is a devastating but infrequent complication of PRRT. The incidence of t-MDS with PRRT is estimated to be 2% to 5%, with a median time to onset after the completion of treatment from 12 to 78 months.3Potential risk factors that predispose patients with NETs to t-MDS, such as use of alkylating agents, presence of bone metastases, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation, have been inconsistently implicated across studies.4Patients with certain somatic mutations or clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential may be more inclined to develop t-MDS after PRRT; however, this association remains understudied.5There does not appear to be a dose effect; patients receiving retreatment with PRRT do not appear to have increased incidence of t-MDS compared with PRRT-naive patients.6The prognosis of patients who develop t-MDS is dismal, with median overall survival times just beyond 1 year from the time of diagnosis.3 Hematologic toxic effects of PRRT are typically subacute and reversible. In the randomized NETTER-1 study,7which garnered PRRT its approval for patients with progressive gastroenteropancreatic NETs, the most frequent grade 3 and 4 hematologic adverse events (AEs) were lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia in 9%, 2%, and 1% of cases, respectively.7None of the hematologic AEs were permanent. In a large observational cohort study of more than 600 patients with gastroenteropancreatic and bronchial NETs who underwent PRRT, 10% of patients experienced grade 3 or 4 hematologic AEs.8The most common of these AEs were thrombocytopenia (5% of cases), leukopenia (5%), and anemia (4%). Within 3 months of follow-up, 77% of these AEs resolved. Some cohort studies, however, suggest that hematologic AEs experienced by patients during PRRT can take longer to resolve.9 Aplastic anemia, characterized by a loss of hematopoietic stem cells, typically occurs because of toxins, viral syndromes, immune destruction, or underlying genetic syndromes.10Marrow toxic agents include some antimicrobial therapies (eg, chloramphenicol), chemotherapy, or high doses of ionizing radiation. Although this patient received ionizing radiation via PRRT, her bone marrow had only mild hypocellularity and no dysplastic features. In the setting of progressive disease, absence of other cytoreductive options and high tumor programmed death-ligand 1 expression, the patient began immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with pembrolizumab. Her anemia and thrombocytopenia are being managed with regular transfusions while disease response reassessment is pending.
